pr_body: Closes #4901 Release Notes: - Added ability to show all diagnostics rendered in an editor Some quick examples of what these look like when rendered: This PR changes Editor::active_diagnostics from `Option` to `HashMap` so that we can track multiple diagnostics groups. Toggling all diagnostics on or off displays or hides all active diagnostics in the current editor. GoToDiagnostic and GoToPrevDiagnostic still support moving through each diagnostic individually while also maintaining the existing behavior single diagnostic view when Show All Diagnostics is off. There aren't any tests associated with this PR because I frankly have no idea where or how to add tests for GUI application. Given that `cargo test --all-targets` only runs 22 tests, I'm guessing I'm poking the test button wrong. In any case, manual testing and normal usage appear to show that its working as intended. Some notes for Zed devs: * I preemptively added the ability to style background colors for diagnostic messages based on severity. I have no idea if there's a process for adding theme-able elements, and the default colors I used kinda clash with my current theme. If there's a process for that I've got no problem reverting those changes. * I picked `F9` as the hotkey for the toggle. I didn't see it bound anywhere else. I have no idea if there's a better default based on other editors or not. * Related to the keybinding, I also added a menu item for the toggle, but it doesn't change state and is awkwardly greyed out when not focused on an editor. I'm guessing that setting probably needs to be moved out of the Editor instance and into some global configuration thinger. * Updating diagnostic displays on every keypress can get a bit wonky. I probably need to add a delayed/debounce task thing that waits for some configurable amount of time after the last refresh request to avoid the visual noise.

[Not a dev, just a fellow Zed-head sliding into your mentions] This looks terrific, @davisp, thanks! It seems a very sensible approach to start by essentially showing all the 'next problem' diagnostics at once. There are possible refinements to make, of course, but by invoking the awesome power of Cunningham's Law, you've got the truck rolling. Appreciate it.

It's always hard to get any PR accepted, and I have a feeling this one will slip down easier if you separate out the colour-theming stuff. That's a great thing to have, too, but it's just a lot to swallow in a single PR. Once we _have_ "show all diagnostics", it's relatively easy to add colour theming to it afterwards. But I'm just bloviating: let's see what the devs say.

@bitfield Thanks for the review! And spot on with this being not quite right but hopefully close enough to the ballpark that a core dev can point me in the right direction to get it across the finish line. I'll try and find some time this weekend to work on getting the configuration settled along with a debounce configuration added as I think those are likely the two biggest issues at this point.

I can't decide which direction to go with the theming stuff. I totally agree with you about getting it in will likely be easier without it, but its not much code so I think I'll just leave it for now. I'd be more than happy to remove it if asked, but if it all goes in at once that seems slightly preferable.

This feature is a dealbreaker.
Sticking with Goland for now until its done - which hopefully will happen asap bc goland sucks.

> Diagnostics text lines can also be very long, what will current impl do then? Scroll, wrap?

One thing that's very neat about Error Lens is that it shows the diagnostic _on the same line_ (at the end), not between lines:

![](https://i.sstatic.net/nGrYS.png)

This is important, because it means the code you're looking at does not move, and it doesn't jump around as the diagnostics change. I think we'd need to do the same thing, otherwise this feature would be quite visually jarring to use. This also solves the offset issue.

The downside is that maybe you can't see the full text of the diagnostic because it doesn't wrap. But the trade-off is worth it. After all, if you want the _full_ diagnostic you can always hover. The key speedup from Error Lens is that you can usually see enough of the error message to be able to fix it.

> One thing that's very neat about Error Lens is that it shows the diagnostic on the same line (at the end), not between lines

The arguments for having the first line of the diagnostic at the end of the line are good, but I for one quite like having them as a new block (old Xcode-style) so I would appreciate at least having that as an option.

This starts to get stale so I'll close it and emphasize again that the hardest part here is not even technical: we need to understand how multiple long line diagnostics are displayed on the same line; same as other pathological cases.

The PR looks quite good overall, so it might serve as a base for future improvements, if anyone wants to take a stab later.

Apologies for taking so long to respond, I ended up getting busy with work and haven't gotten around to updating this PR as far as I would have liked.

For some top line context, I've been using this branch of zed as my daily driver for editing Rust full time and I am 100% on board with the fact that this is absolutely not ready for prime time. The diagnostic display is both atrocious and bumpy. Not being a UI dev at all I hadn't even considered the flickering issue in regards to accessibility stuff which is enough to ixnay this PR on its own IMO.

Also, given that context, I wouldn't be using Zed at all without this branch. I think there are enough other folks echoing that sentiment that I don't really need to underline how important *something* of this nature is desired whether or not there's agreement on the specifics (inline vs blocks).

And now on to responding to the review to provide some more context for others.

> My main issue with the PR is how large amounts of diagnostics are displayed.

I'm 100% in agreement here. However, I want to be clear that the current state of affairs weird duplicates and their sometimes odd positioning is not due to this PR. (Well, other than I didn't change anything to fix the issue I guess).

This entire PR can be succinctly summarized as "Rather than having to press F8 to cycle through diagnostics individually, let me toggle them all on at once". That is to say, in the examples shown, those are all real diagnostics that would be cycled through and displayed exactly the same. I've wondered a couple times while using this if I didn't introduce a duplications somewhere when its egregious, but each time I turn off the show all, I still cycle through all of them.

That's to say, those are the diagnostics as they exist for the F8 cycling behavior. Any work on de-duplicating those will likely require some spelunking between the Editor and however the plumbing to LSP land works.

One other thing I'll point out is that the reason that this branch shows diagnostics as blocks is simply because that's how F8 works. I have absolutely no idea how one would do the magical "show diagnostic text on the same line" similar to inlay hints or whatever. I assume I could figure it out eventually, but in terms of time my crap approach was enough to get me using Zed full time so that was good enough for me.

> * F9 does not work reliably: see my comments below, it needs a test.
>   This leaves the feeling that updates are quite slow, since nothing is refreshed onscreen.

I think this is two issues after having used this quite a lot. F9 itself works fine. I've never had it not work. However, I have had a few encounters where the diagnostics got so bad I had to toggle Show All to fix whatever I was working on before re-enabling due to latency and other issues. Performance is absolutely part of why I don't think this PR is any where near mergeable.

> * I found it confusing that `ESC` does not work and does not toggle off these diagnostics — most (if not all) of the editor blocks in Zed (e.g. diff views and inline assistant code blocks) disappear after it's pressed and I think we should do it for the new blocks too.

I believe this fundamentally misunderstands what most folks want out of this feature. The entire point is that these diagnostics are shown all the time forever and for always (well, except for when turning off the feature). But they are absolutely not a modal to be dismissed. Think of it like an instantaneous compiler loop. If the compiler says something won't compile, it gets highlighted in bright colors with hopefully enough context presented to address the issue without leaving the editor (or slightly less worse, having to hover over a target). Whether that's inline a la Code Lens style, or as blocks is secondary (and should probably be configurable if I'm being honest).

> As noted in the PR message, flickers are quite hazardous and we need to fix them:

Point absolutely acknowledged! I'm not a UI dev so I didn't even consider the UI/Accessibility aspect there, but that's yet another nail in this PR's coffin.

I'll respond to a few of the other inline comments as well, though given this specific PR is dead in the water, I'll skip the obvious changes as there's nothing I disagree with in the requested changes.

No worries and thank you for testing that yourself, that is the main part (followed by the ability to fix the issues, of course).
I was not so swift to provide the feedback anyway, so no rush.

Regarding the F8 feedback and diagnostics displayed, I would wait until https://github.com/zed-industries/zed/tree/overhaul-multibuffer lands to see how the new multi buffer will behave: if we can extend its excerpts easier and merge them on the fly, we might be able to show all diagnostics at once, jump between them and be quite close to regular buffer(s).
That is not the replacement, but somehow an alternative to some people, at least.

Roger the ESC idea, albeit I suspect the future user feedback will converge us into that mode, just later.
I'd keep that in mind when renaming the settings, and added the enum "always"/"never" instead of a boolean as it is now.
So that later someone could fit that behavior into the setting easier.

I think if we fix the

> The diagnostic display is both atrocious and bumpy. Not being a UI dev at all I hadn't even considered the flickering issue in regards to accessibility stuff which is enough to ixnay this PR on its own IMO.

and whatever brings "stuck" F9 feeling, this will be a perfect first iteration on the topic, given that we also add some logical "unit" tests that show/hide the diagnostics and check the editor (?) data changes (so no UI things).

I would also not put much work into customizing the diagnostics view, but concentrated on grouping and layouting them so that it's normal to read the code somehow.
If we group the items "logically", that will cut off half of the sinister appeal at least.

From that experience, I'd personally see that it would make sense to implement this as a built-in option (i.e. no extension), with implementation steps being the following:

1. Refactoring of the current diagnostic system to support having multiple diagnostics open at the same time: currently only one can be visible at once. If you've never used Error Lens, it's really surprising what a difference it makes to your workflow. You might think "What's the big deal? I can always hover the mouse over the squiggly line and see the error, or press F8 to go to 'next problem'." But that's an action _I_ have to take, and I've noticed my students quite happily ignoring the squiggly line indicators, trying to run the program, and then being surprised that it doesn't compile.

As soon as I tell them to turn on Error Lens (in VS Code), that issue disappears, because every error and warning is shown right IN THEIR FACES, unavoidably, unignorably. It's like seeing the teacher's red pen all over your code. And it helps me too, because eliminating that one extra step makes a big difference. 

Writing Rust, you see errors and warnings _all the time_: it's like a constant, ongoing dialogue between you and the compiler. The Error Lens facility just removes the friction from that loop: type something, see the error, fix the mistake. Since it's something that all language-server-supported scopes can benefit from, this feature seems well worth it.

Right, so this just got simplified out due to how I added support for showing all diagnostics. The basic idea here is a standard set update. I have an old set of diagnostics (whatever is currently being shown) and the new set (whatever the LSP has just sent us). The idea is only hide diagnostics that no longer exist while only adding newly encountered diagnostics. The standard optimization over "hide all old ones, show all new ones" sort of optimization.

The `is_valid` is just doing the same thing except since it only ever cared about a single diagnostic group at once its doing the "what to remove/what to add" logic directly at the individual diagnostic level rather than at the group_id level that I added for showing all diagnostics. I just reused the same logic since it simplified things a bit at the cost of storing that list in the `self.active_diagnostics` HashMap.

I find it quite suspicious that we have to do something relatively complex (as iterating over all diagnostics and updating them) when they go in/out of focus.

Could we avoid any diagnostics update and use the old data instead?

Whoops. That's totally me making another "See, I'm totally not a UI dev" mistake. The focus/unfocus is a bad name I picked for changing which of the diagnostics `F8` is currently pointing at. I tried to keep it so that if you were searching around F8 style and then toggled the F9 version on and off, the F8 progress/state wouldn't be lost. Oh and also so that F8 can jump to next diagnostic even when F9 is on, which I think is where focus came from (i.e., scroll next one into view). In hindsight, I could see how a real UI person would immediately think window focus/unfocus instead.

As to the specific question on optimizations, my vague memory is "I could optimize this by duplicating some of the logic in refresh_active_diagnostics, or I could just take the (possible, unmeasured, maybe zero) performance hit in completely re-running the refresh logic." Also, this unfocus is only ever called when users dismiss the active F8 style diagnostic and we're already running refresh_active_diagnostics on every key stroke, so :shrug: on that performance hit.
